extracted.intended_audience: persons engaged in collecting oological (birds' eggs) specimens; amateur and practicing naturalists/egg-collectors
extracted.subtask_description: Practical instructions and best practices for preparing, cleaning, labelling, and storing birds' eggs for cabinets and exchanges, including equipment use and exceptions for delicate shells. Aimed at field collectors and cabinet curators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare your eggs neat and clean
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare your eggs neat and clean. There is no excuse for having a dirty set of eggs where water, soap, and a tooth-brush can be found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wash eggs with water, soap and a toothbrush. Exception: some eggs (mostly water-birds; Smithsonian catalogue numbers referenced) have very calcareous shells whose characteristic markings will wash away — these should not be washed. Having once seen such shells you will not mistake them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make but one hole, and that a small one in the middle of the egg
rubrics_metrics.description: Make but one hole, and that a small one in the middle of the egg; cover this hole, when the contents are removed, and the specimen is dry, with gold-beater skin or the paper number indicating the bird.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an egg drill or a pointed wire of four or six sides to make the opening. Do not blow with two holes (one each end); modern practice is a single small central hole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a blowpipe (and water injection) to remove egg contents
rubrics_metrics.description: If the blowpipe does not readily remove the contents of the egg, inject water and shake the specimen thoroughly, then blow again, and repeat the operation until every particle of the egg is removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeat injection/shaking/blowing until entirely empty. Ensure removal of all internal material to avoid later staining or odour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for eggs with advanced embryos
rubrics_metrics.description: If the embryo is too far advanced to remove through a moderate sized hole, blow out what you can of the liquid part and fill the egg with water, wipe it dry and put it away in a covered box in some warm place, and every twenty-four or forty-eight hours shake it well and remove what you can, and then refill with water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeat this operation several times; after a few days the contents will become sufficiently decomposed to take away. This is the recommended method when embryo cannot be removed by simple blowing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thoroughly cleanse the shell after emptying
rubrics_metrics.description: After removing the contents of any egg, cleanse the shell thoroughly. Fill it with clean water and shake vigorously, blow out the contents and repeat the operation until the specimen is perfectly clean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly desirable for white eggs because black spots will show through the shell later if any particle of egg or blood remains inside. Repeat until perfectly clean.

rubrics_metrics.name: Save all your eggs in sets (keep clutch together)
rubrics_metrics.description: Save all your eggs in sets—that is, keep all the eggs each bird lays by themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keeping sets is the only way to form a correct knowledge of the eggs of any species because single eggs can be misleading; great variation may occur even within one nest (example: four eggs of the same nest two pure white and two blotched).

rubrics_metrics.name: Record place and date for each set
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep a memorandum of the place and date of collecting each set of eggs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate locality and date data are essential for the scientific value of the collection and for correct species/variation records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and maintain an appropriate blowpipe instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: Use some kind of blowpipe in preparing your eggs for the cabinet. The common blowpipe, with a fine pointed tip, will answer; but a thumb-and-finger operated blowpipe (E. W. Ellsworth's) works expeditiously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take care of the instrument: if leather packing dries, work the instrument submerged in warm soap suds to restore pliability. Printed directions accompanying the instrument should be sufficient for repairs; consult the maker for further information. Warning: manual blowing can tax lungs and cause dizziness — use suitable instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production quality for natural-history books (paper, printing, binding)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mode in which the work is got out—the paper, the printing, and the binding—leaves nothing to be desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High production standards (good paper, clear printing, strong binding) are essential; they materially affect the value and usability of a natural-history book for its intended readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustration quality and appropriateness in books
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrations should be accurate botanical drawings and well executed; smaller figures may be equally good to larger ones, but avoid superfluous illustrations that do not add unique information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Botanical illustrations by skilled artists (example: Mr. Worthington Smith) are valuable; however, unnecessary drawings (e.g., garden roller and water-pot with no unique features) may be spared. Balance completeness with relevance to promote usefulness and reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographic printing for natural-history illustration: fidelity and aesthetic
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographic printing modes (Albert and Woodbury processes) can portray every marking on the surface of specimens with the accuracy of nature printing and with the beauty of a lithograph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-fidelity photographic reproduction that captures fine surface markings and aesthetic quality should be preferred for natural-history works; such methods may revolutionise specimen illustration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents of a valuable fisheries/commerce report
rubrics_metrics.description: A valuable report upon commerce in the products of the sea describes the different marketable products in detail and indicates the relative rank which they occupy in commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include area, population, most important ports, commercial tonnage of principal nations; imports and exports of sea products showing market capacity and supplying countries; catch, consumption, and balance of trade from official statistics. Such comprehensive data make the report a valuable contribution to fisheries statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plantation/report metrics for Cinchona (or plantation reports generally)
rubrics_metrics.description: Report on plantations should state growth and health of plants (height and girth), identify species introduced and their suitability, quantify supplies of raw material (lbs of fresh bark supplied), and estimate expected yield per tree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include economic calculations (yield per tree, price per lb, clear profit per lb) to assess commercial viability. Example figures supplied: heights 22–30 ft, girths 18 in–3 ft, 51,353 lbs fresh bark supplied, expected yields and profit estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectives and components of a geological field excursion
rubrics_metrics.description: Excursions should be planned to afford opportunity to study specified strata (e.g., Silurian and Cambrian), examine exposures, outcrops, important limestones and shales, fossiliferous sections, and physiography of districts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a schedule of sites and leaders, identify specific formations and localities to be inspected (e.g., Upper Ludlow, Aymestry Limestone, Wenlock Shale, junctions of Cambrian and Silurian), and ensure activities (walking routes, quarry inspection) target pedagogic goals for students of the relevant rocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value criteria for papers in geological and microscopical journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal issues should include important illustrated articles, descriptions of new species, revisions of genera, criticisms of previous memoirs, and communications introducing improved methods or instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A valuable issue mixes original descriptive work (new taxa, revisions), methodological advances (e.g., improved illuminators), illustrative plates, and critical discussion; brief notices and society proceedings also serve the community.
